prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms are held at a magic wavelength so that many neutral atoms are interrogated without Doppler or recoil shifts, reaching fractional uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: I have moved from B012 to B018 after the first round. The question I always ask is what the essential mechanism is and who identified it. For the lattice clock the answer is simple and general: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, and a lattice can hold thousands of atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime without perturbing the transition. That is a new physical idea about light shifts, not a tuning of the comb (2005, a ruler for optical frequencies) or of single-ion control (2012, one quantum system with a very small signal). The gain comes from statistics over many atoms combined with systematic control, which is a different route to the performance. It is also checked and not just claimed: Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others reproduce the performance on several species, and inter-laboratory comparisons exist. Katori is the originator of the magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstration. Ye's group took accuracy and coherence to the 1e-18 level and to many-body clock operation, and that work is not comb infrastructure. A two-name credit means no forced exclusions. I would write the magic wavelength and many-atom interrogation into the citation so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is on the page.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which Kroll, Olsson and Danielsson raised in different words, is that the lattice clock sits next to two earlier precision-measurement prizes and that the 1e-18 figure is a performance record, not a surprising fact about nature. I find the physics distinct enough to answer this, but I cannot prove that every colleague will. Olsson's rule, that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation, puts pressure on Ye's share, and the committee must be able to say why Ye is more than a refiner of Katori's concept. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups stay outside the two names. The redefinition of the second is still pending. Finally, B012, my own first choice in round 1, remains scientifically the cleaner mechanism and the better-understood result, so I give it up mainly because of thin support, the 2016 overlap and the lack of a laboratory before-and-after, not because the science is weaker.

responses.point: Olsson's rule is that the prize should go to the original experiment, not to a second discoverer who did it much better, and she asks whether Ye's role is decisive enough to share the prize with Katori.
responses.response: I share the rule, and I applied a version of it myself when I asked to separate Katori's concept from the accuracy campaign. I think the rule is satisfied here, but only if the citation is framed as you suggest, around the lattice clock as a new type of instrument. Katori holds the idea and the first strontium realisation. Ye's group did more than improve a number: its record accuracy and its demonstration of coherent many-body interrogation showed what the lattice makes possible. That is a physical contribution to understanding the platform, not only a better realisation. I would record this reasoning in our discussion, as you propose, so the exclusion of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley rests on a stated argument.

responses.point: Johansson asked me for experimental evidence for the two-step melting scenario beyond colloids and simulation, and noted that first-order melting in some systems weakens the case for B012.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and it affects my decision. The evidence I can cite from memory is two-dimensional colloidal and superparamagnetic monolayers, where two-stage melting with an intermediate hexatic phase was seen, plus liquid-crystal films and simulation. I also know of later hard-disk simulations that find a first-order liquid-hexatic transition, so the scenario is system-dependent, as I conceded. I cannot claim that the universal picture is confirmed to the standard that the lattice clock meets with many independent laboratories and quantitative inter-laboratory comparisons. Together with the 2016 overlap, this is the main reason I no longer insist on B012.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether Ye's share is the accuracy and many-body work or also comb infrastructure, and wants the citation to state lattice clock and magic wavelength so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is explicit.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording and have put the magic wavelength and many-atom interrogation into mine. On Ye's share, I would credit the accuracy, coherence and many-body clock work, and I would not credit comb infrastructure, since that belongs to the 2005 prize. I would say this openly in discussion so that the objection about Ye's comb heritage is addressed and not avoided. I also disagree with waiting for the redefinition of the second: that depends on a metrology committee's calendar, and the scientific case is already complete.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 fails on the physics, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a new trapping principle for interrogating thousands of neutral atoms, and the pending redefinition is a reason to prize it now.
responses.response: As a theorist from outside atomic physics I find that argument convincing in terms of mechanism. A condition under which a perturbation cancels, so that an ensemble behaves like a single well-isolated quantum system, is the kind of simple general idea I trust. I would still ask you and Pearce to have an expert reviewer confirm the 1e-18 uncertainty budgets and the inter-laboratory comparisons before the final ballot, since none of us can verify the current record from these files.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B038 as a mature, overdue discovery, while acknowledging that his own case could fail on attribution alone.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the science and I take the overdue argument seriously, but I think you have identified the problem correctly. The X-ray localisation by Costa and Frontera is clear. The optical transient and redshift came from several groups within weeks, so any triple, including Kulkarni's, is a selection among many. Until a concrete eligible and decisive set is named, I would not put B038 ahead of a candidate whose credit is settled by two names. I would keep it as a candidate for a later year if an expert report on attribution supports a specific set.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution is read by the committee as original physics or as a better realisation of Katori's concept, which decides whether the pair or Katori alone is defensible.
Whether the record uncertainties and inter-laboratory comparisons are as I recall them; I rely on colleagues' statements and have no expert verification.

Whether B012 should be tested again in a later year if the committee decides that the 2016 overlap is not a problem; my recall of the Halperin-Nelson and Young priority and of the hard-disk first-order results is not independently checked.
Whether the committee prefers a two-part structure, such as B018 with B012, which would cost names beyond the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori, Ye, or any candidate in the preferred configuration. I have no recorded collaboration with them. B012, now my alternative, is close to my own statistical-physics field, but I have no link to Young, Halperin or Nelson. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (GU and Chalmers) and know of no specific conflict regarding any shortlisted candidate.
